title: 2  ggplot intro
text:
2.1 The layer skeleton
A ggplot call builds up in layers. ggplot doesn’t care what order you write them in — + just adds elements to the plot object — but writing them in this order mirrors the underlying grammar and keeps calls readable.
# data + global (inherited) mapping
ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = xvar, y = yvar)) +   
  
  # geom: aes() = mapped, arg = fixed
  geom_col(aes(fill = grp), colour = "black") +         
  # stat = "identity" is geom_col's default; 
  # use geom_bar(stat = "count") to let ggplot tally rows

  # scale: controls how mapped values -> visual controls
  scale_fill_manual(values = my_palette) +      
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +

  # coord: alters the coordinate space (e.g. horizontal bars)
  coord_flip() +                                          

  # facet: splits into small multiples
  facet_wrap(~ facet_var, scales = "free_y") +             

  labs(title = "Title", x = "X axis", y = "Y axis", fill = "Legend") +

  # theme: non-data styling, best applied last
  theme_minimal() +                                       
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: 2  ggplot intro
text:
2.2 Setting aesthetics aes
The one conceptual distinction worth keeping straight, since it’s the actual source of bugs:
Mapped vs fixed.

aes(colour = var) maps a column to a visual property — it varies row to row.

colour = "black" outside aes() sets it to one fixed value for the whole layer.

Global vs local.

aes() supplied inside ggplot() is inherited by every geom that follows.

aes() supplied inside a specific geom_*() only applies to that layer, and overrides the global mapping for that aesthetic.

title: 2  ggplot intro
text:
2.3 Presentation vs calculation of statistics
Different ggplot geoms approach this differently. Some calculate new statistics on the data you pass them, others simply plot the data already there.

geom_bar() uses stat ‘count’ to count the number of cases in x category,

geom_col() uses stat ‘identity’. It plots the values already in y; bar height = y,

geom_boxplot() does much more, it calculates IQR, median, max and min, and presents them all,

geom_histogram() bins continuous variables and counts the observations per bin.

These are controlled by the stat argument, which defines the calculation used.

title: 2  ggplot intro
text:
2.4 Applied examples
Worked against mpg and economics_long, both built into ggplot2 — no external data needed to reproduce any of these.







Concept
Illustrated with




x / y axis
geom_point


Colour vs fill
geom_col


Stat: calculated vs pre-supplied
geom_bar → geom_col → geom_histogram


Position adjustments
geom_col


Axis reordering
geom_col


Continuous vs discrete colours
geom_point


Size
geom_point


Shape
geom_point


Alpha (transparency)
geom_point


Linetype
geom_line


Group
geom_line (+ spaghetti plot)


Data labels
geom_col + geom_text


Facets
geom_boxplot


Overlaying geoms
geom_boxplot + geom_jitter




library(tidyverse)


2.4.1 x / y axis
The two positional aesthetics. Both continuous here. Each point’s screen position is read straight off the data.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()










2.4.2 Colour vs fill
colour is the outline, fill the fill colour.

mpg_class <- mpg %>% count(class)

ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  # fill = bar interior, colour = bar outline — both visible at once
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_flip()










2.4.3 Stat: calculated vs pre-supplied
Below we have the same chart, arrived at in two ways.
geom_bar takes raw rows and counts them; geom_col takes a value that’s already been counted.

# geom_bar: raw rows in, ggplot counts them (stat = "count")
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")








Here stat is created separately using count(), then presented with geom_col().

# geom_col: pre-aggregated, ggplot just plots n (stat = "identity")
mpg_class <- mpg %>% count(class)
ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")








There are lots of statistics ggplot can calculate on the back end, for example, a third stat type — geom_histogram bins a continuous variable, then counts rows per bin (stat = “bin”):

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")










2.4.4 Position adjustments
Same grouped data, three ways to arrange the fill segments within each bar.

mpg_class_drv <- mpg %>% count(class, drv)

# stack (default): segments sit on top of each other
ggplot(mpg_class_drv, aes(x = class, y = n, fill = drv)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  coord_flip()







# dodge: segments sit side by side
ggplot(mpg_class_drv, aes(x = class, y = n, fill = drv)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip()







# fill: stacked and rescaled to proportions (0-1) — good for share-of-total
ggplot(mpg_class_drv, aes(x = class, y = n, fill = drv)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  coord_flip()










2.4.5 Axis reordering
Discrete axes default to factor/alphabetical order, which is rarely what you want on a ranked bar chart.

# default: alphabetical
ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()







# reordered by value
ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = fct_reorder(class, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "class")










2.4.6 Continuous vs discrete colours
Same aesthetic (colour), different variable type — the scale and legend change accordingly.

# continuous -> gradient legend
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = cty)) +
  geom_point()







# discrete -> key legend
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = class)) +
  geom_point()










2.4.7 Size

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = cty)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6)










2.4.8 Shape
Discrete only, point geoms only — and unreadable much past 5-6 levels. drv has three.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, shape = drv)) +
  geom_point(size = 2)










2.4.9 Alpha (transparency)
Fixed here rather than mapped — every point equally transparent, which is what you want for overplotting.
Some appear darker here - this is because some points overlap. This is what alpha is telling you.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 3)









Here you can see the overlap increasing opacity.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.3, size = 3)










2.4.10 Linetype

econ_subset <- economics_long %>% filter(variable %in% c("psavert", "uempmed"))

ggplot(econ_subset, aes(x = date, y = value01, linetype = variable)) +
  geom_line()










2.4.11 Group
The classic bug: with no colour or group mapping, ggplot draws one line straight through every row in row order not one line per series.

# broken: one zigzag line through all five series
ggplot(economics_long, aes(x = date, y = value01)) +
  geom_line()







# fixed: group (or colour) tells ggplot to draw one line per series
ggplot(economics_long, aes(x = date, y = value01, group = variable)) +
  geom_line()








Spaghetti plot — many individual trajectories, no colour. The standard diagnostic for repeated-measures/panel data before fitting a mixed model: one line per respondent, group = id, deliberately not mapped to colour (colouring 30+ respondents just produces an unreadable legend).

set.seed(1)
panel_data <- tibble(
  id   = rep(1:30, each = 5),
  wave = rep(1:5, times = 30)
) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(score = 50 + (wave - 1) * rnorm(1, 2, 1) + rnorm(1, 0, 8) + rnorm(5, 0, 4)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(panel_data, aes(x = wave, y = score, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3)










2.4.12 Data labels
Putting the value directly on the chart — geom_text() (or geom_label() for a background box) layered on top of another geom.

ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.3) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off")








Labelling individual scatter points is a different problem — points overlap, so a bare geom_text() produces unreadable clutter. The standard fix is the ggrepel package (geom_text_repel() / geom_label_repel()), which nudges overlapping labels apart automatically. Not demonstrated here since it needs an extra package, but it’s the first thing to reach for the moment point labels overlap.


2.4.13 Facets

# facet_wrap: one variable, wrapped into a grid
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ drv)







# facet_grid: two variables, strict rows x columns
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(drv ~ year)










2.4.14 Overlaying geoms
Layers stack — nothing stops you combining two geoms on the same data to get the benefit of both. Here, the boxplot’s summary shape plus every individual observation from geom_jitter. outlier.shape = NA turns off the boxplot’s own outlier points so they don’t get drawn twice (once by the boxplot, once by jitter).

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3, colour = "blue")

title: 3  Geom gallery
text:
A single, basic worked example of each geom on the original “core-ish” list — standalone from the intro chapter, so nothing here depends on objects created there. Worked against mpg and economics, both built into ggplot2, plus ggrepel for the two repel geoms (install.packages("ggrepel") if not already installed).

library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)


3.0.1 geom_point

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()










3.0.2 geom_line

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line()










3.0.3 geom_col / geom_bar
geom_bar counts raw rows for you (stat "count"); geom_col plots a value you’ve already computed (stat "identity").

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")







mpg_class <- mpg %>% count(class)

ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")










3.0.4 Grouped bar chart
position = "dodge" — one bar per drivetrain, side by side within each class. Flipped horizontal here (coord_flip()), which is the usual fix once category labels get too long to sit legibly on the x axis.

mpg_class_drv <- mpg %>% count(class, drv)

ggplot(mpg_class_drv, aes(x = class, y = n, fill = drv)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip()










3.0.5 Stacked bar chart
position = "stack" — ggplot’s default for geom_col/geom_bar when fill is mapped, so it doesn’t need to be stated explicitly. Same data as the grouped chart above, segments stacked into one bar per class instead of sitting side by side.

ggplot(mpg_class_drv, aes(x = class, y = n, fill = drv)) +
  geom_col()










3.0.6 geom_histogram

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue", colour = "black")










3.0.7 geom_density

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = hwy)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5)










3.0.8 geom_boxplot

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() 








 With an overlay…

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.2, colour = "blue")










3.0.9 geom_violin
Same shape of comparison as the boxplot above, but shows the full distribution shape rather than just the five-number summary.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = hwy)) +
  geom_violin() 










3.0.10 geom_jitter
cty vs a discrete x — plain points would stack exactly on top of each other; jitter adds a small amount of random noise so overlapping observations are visible.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, y = cty)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5)










3.0.11 geom_smooth
A fitted trend line with its confidence ribbon, layered over the raw points.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'











3.0.12 geom_errorbar / geom_pointrange
Uncertainty around a point estimate — here, mean hwy by class ± 1 standard error.

mpg_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy), se_hwy = sd(hwy) / sqrt(n()))

ggplot(mpg_summary, aes(x = class, y = mean_hwy)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_hwy - se_hwy, ymax = mean_hwy + se_hwy), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point()







# geom_pointrange does the same thing in a single geom
ggplot(mpg_summary, aes(x = class, y = mean_hwy)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean_hwy - se_hwy, ymax = mean_hwy + se_hwy))










3.0.13 geom_area / geom_ribbon
geom_area fills the space under a single line; geom_ribbon fills the space between two values (ymin/ymax) — here an illustrative ±10% band around the same series.

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_area(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6)







ggplot(economics, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = unemploy * 0.9, ymax = unemploy * 1.1), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = unemploy))










3.0.14 geom_text / geom_label
Value labels placed directly on a chart — geom_label adds a background box, geom_text doesn’t.

ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.3)







ggplot(mpg_class, aes(x = class, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", colour = "black") +
  geom_label(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.3)










3.0.15 geom_text_repel / geom_label_repel (ggrepel)
Plain geom_text on a scatter plot produces overlapping, unreadable labels. ggrepel’s versions nudge labels apart automatically while keeping a leader line back to the point.

mpg_class_means <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(displ = mean(displ), hwy = mean(hwy))

ggplot(mpg_class_means, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, label = class)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text_repel()










3.0.16 geom_tile
The actual case for reaching for this: a correlation matrix. A table of numbers is slow to scan for pattern; colour lets your eye pick out the strong relationships immediately, and overlaying the coefficient keeps the precision a table gives you. Same logic applies to any variable-by-variable or category-by-category grid — cross-tab percentages, a similarity matrix, a confusion matrix.

mtcars_cor <- mtcars %>%
  select(mpg, disp, hp, drat, wt, qsec) %>%
  cor() %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "correlation")

ggplot(mtcars_cor, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

title: 4  Layering a plot, stage by stage
text:
The skeleton in the intro chapter shows the full anatomy of a ggplot call at once. This chapter rebuilds it one layer at a time on a single running example — diamonds (built into ggplot2) — so the effect of each addition is visible on its own before the next one goes on.
The question: how does the mix of cut quality within each clarity grade change, and does that composition differ by colour grade? This is a share question, not a volume one — and that shapes several of the choices made from stage 2 onward.

4.0.1 The data
diamonds is ~54,000 round-cut diamonds with price and nine physical/quality attributes. Three of those are the ones in play here, and all three are graded, ordered categories rather than arbitrary labels:

cut — quality of the cut: Fair (worst), Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal (best)
color — diamond colour grade: D (best, colourless) through J (worst, most visible tint)
clarity — how free of inclusions the stone is: I1 (worst) through IF (best, internally flawless)

None of these are things you’d normally sum or average directly — they’re categorical groupings, which is exactly the shape of variable a bar chart is for. diamonds_summary collapses the ~54,000 individual diamonds down to one row per combination of the three, with n giving the count of diamonds in each — that’s what gets plotted throughout, not the raw data.
Neither clarity nor color reads as obviously ordered from its labels alone — nothing about “I1” or “D” tells a viewer which end is best. Rather than fixing that with scale/labeller code at every plotting stage, it’s simplest to relabel the two extreme levels once, in the data, before any plot is built — fct_recode() renames a factor level without disturbing its position in the level order, so every chart from here on inherits the tagged labels automatically.

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)


diamonds_summary <- diamonds %>%
  count(clarity, cut, color) %>%
  mutate(
    clarity = fct_recode(clarity, "I1 (worst)" = "I1", "IF (best)" = "IF"),
    color   = fct_recode(color,   "D (best)" = "D",   "J (worst)" = "J")
  )



4.0.2 1. Create plot
Just x and y mapped, default geom settings. With no fill mapped, geom_col’s default position = "stack" silently collapses the cut/color breakdown into one bar per clarity grade — this is the total count per clarity. It’s a real number, but it doesn’t answer the actual question: it says nothing about how the mix of cut quality shifts from one clarity grade to the next, since clarity grades have wildly different total volumes to begin with.

plot <- ggplot(diamonds_summary, aes(x = clarity, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

plot










4.0.3 2. fill colour
fill = cut is mapped — it varies by row, splitting each bar into its cut segments. But comparing segment sizes across bars only works if every bar is the same total height — otherwise a clarity grade with more diamonds overall will always look like it has “more” of every cut, regardless of the actual mix. position = "fill" rescales every bar to 100%, so segment proportions become directly comparable across clarity grades.
Confusingly, “fill” means two different things in this one call: aes(fill = cut) is the aesthetic being coloured by; position = "fill" is the position adjustment that rescales and stacks. Same word, unrelated arguments.

plot <- ggplot(diamonds_summary, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill")

plot








The composition story is already visible here in a way stage 1 couldn’t show: better clarity grades visibly carry a larger share of Ideal/Premium cuts.


4.0.4 3. Colour palette
Swapping ggplot’s default hue palette for a deliberate one.

cut_palette <- c(
  "Fair"      = "#b2182b",
  "Good"      = "#ef8a62",
  "Very Good" = "#fddbc7",
  "Premium"   = "#67a9cf",
  "Ideal"     = "#2166ac"
)

plot <- plot +  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_palette)
plot










4.0.5 4. Axis scale
The y-axis is a proportion now (0 to 1), not a raw count — scales::comma is the right tool for large counts, but it’s the wrong one here. scales::percent matches what the axis actually represents.

plot <- plot +  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)
plot










4.0.6 5. Axis flip
clarity’s labels are short enough to survive on a vertical axis here, but this is the point in the build where you’d reach for coord_flip() if they weren’t — horizontal bars, category labels read left to right instead of rotated.

plot <- plot +  coord_flip()
plot










4.0.7 6. Add facets
Splitting into one panel per colour grade answers the second half of the original question directly: does the cut composition pattern seen above hold across colour grades, or does it shift? The “(best)”/“(worst)” tags on the two extreme colour grades — baked into the data up front — carry straight through to the facet strip labels here with no extra code.

plot <- plot + facet_wrap(~ color, scales = "free_x")
plot 








The gotcha worth flagging separately: after coord_flip(), free_x/free_y in facet_wrap() swap meaning. Facet scales are evaluated on the physical, post-flip axes — not on the original x/y aesthetic roles the way theme elements are. Since the share axis (n, rescaled by position = "fill") now renders horizontally, it’s scales = "free_x" that frees it per panel, not "free_y" — easy to get backwards.


4.0.8 7. Label plot

plot <- plot +
  labs(
    title = "Cut composition by clarity, faceted by colour grade",
    x     = "Clarity",
    y     = "Share of diamonds",
    fill  = "Cut"
  )

plot










4.0.9 8. Theme
Non-data styling, applied last, in three passes rather than one jump.
8a — base theme. Swap ggplot’s default grey panel for a plain one.

plot <- plot +  theme_minimal()
plot








8b — legend placement and sizing. Seven facets and five cut categories already crowd the plot — move the legend below and shrink the keys so it doesn’t compete with the panels.

plot <- plot  +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )

plot








8c — text sizing and gridline cleanup. The export-ready pass: consistent text sizes across every text element, minor gridlines dropped, facet strip labels tidied.

plot <- plot + 
  theme(
    legend.position   = "bottom",
    legend.key.size   = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.text       = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.title      = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text         = element_text(size = 8, colour = "black"),
    axis.title        = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.title        = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text        = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor  = element_blank()
  )

plot










4.0.10 Putting it all together
The same chart, all stages combined into the one call you’d actually write:

ggplot(diamonds_summary, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +

  # geom: fill mapped (varies by cut). position = "fill" rescales each bar
  # to 100% so cut composition is comparable across clarity grades,
  # regardless of their total volume
  geom_col(position = "fill") +

  # scale: deliberate palette + percent-formatted shares (not comma —
  # this axis is a proportion, not a count)
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +

  # coord: horizontal bars
  coord_flip() +

  # facet: one panel per colour grade — free_x, not free_y, since coord_flip
  # already swapped which physical axis carries the share
  facet_wrap(~ color, scales = "free_x") +

  labs(
    title = "Cut composition by clarity, faceted by colour grade",
    x     = "Clarity",
    y     = "Share of diamonds",
    fill  = "Cut"
  ) +

  # theme: base, then legend, then the export-ready text/gridline pass
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position   = "bottom",
    legend.key.size   = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.text       = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.title      = element_text(size = 9),
    axis.text         = element_text(size = 8, colour = "black"),
    axis.title        = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.title        = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text        = element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor  = element_blank()
  )

title: 5  Theme: what it controls, and the element_ functions
text:
theme() controls every piece of non-data ink on a plot — anything not determined by an aesthetic mapping. It can’t touch scales, coordinates, or geoms; it’s purely visual. Every argument takes one of four element functions.

library(tidyverse)


5.0.1 The areas theme() works on
Text. Every piece of writing on the plot — title, axis labels, legend labels, facet strip labels — can be styled independently, though they all fall back to one shared default if left untouched. e.g. axis.text = element_text(size = 8) shrinks just the tick labels, leaving the title and legend alone.
Axis details. The physical marks that frame an axis — its tick marks and the line running along it — as distinct from the text sitting next to them. e.g. axis.ticks = element_blank() removes the tick marks entirely while the axis text stays put.
Panel. The plotting area itself: its background, border, and the gridlines sitting behind the data — the canvas the geoms are drawn on top of, not the data. e.g. panel.grid.minor = element_blank() drops the finer gridlines, leaving only the major ones for orientation.
Legend. Where the legend sits and how its internal pieces — the coloured swatches, their spacing, their labels — are laid out, entirely separate from what the legend shows (that’s controlled by scale_*()/labs(), not theme()). e.g. legend.position = "bottom" moves the whole legend under the plot instead of to the side.
Facet strips. The small labelled boxes sitting above each facet panel, identifying which subset of the data that panel represents. e.g. strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey85") gives each strip a shaded backing so it stands out from the panel below it.
Plot-level. The outer canvas the entire plot sits on — background and the breathing room around its edges — outside the panel itself. e.g. plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10) adds even padding around the whole thing.
A couple of mechanics worth knowing beyond the individual areas: elements inherit down a hierarchy (setting text cascades to axis.text, legend.text, etc. unless a more specific one overrides it), theme_set() changes the default theme for the rest of a session instead of adding + theme_minimal() everywhere, and %+replace% fully replaces an inherited element rather than merging into it — relevant if building a custom theme rather than tweaking a built-in one.


5.0.2 The element_ functions
element_text() — anything rendered as text. Arguments: family (font), face ("plain"/"bold"/"italic"/"bold.italic"), colour, size (points), hjust/vjust (0–1 justification), angle (degrees), lineheight, margin (spacing around the text itself, via margin()).
element_line() — anything drawn as a line: axis lines, tick marks, gridlines. Arguments: colour, linewidth (renamed from size in ggplot2 3.4+), linetype ("solid"/"dashed"/"dotted"/etc.), lineend ("round"/"butt"/"square"), arrow.
element_rect() — anything filled as a rectangle: panel background, plot background, legend background, facet strip background. Arguments: fill, colour (border), linewidth (border thickness), linetype.
element_blank() — draws nothing, and takes no arguments. Removing an element this way also frees the space it would have occupied — the difference from setting colour = "transparent" or fill = NA, which keep the element’s footprint.


5.0.3 Seeing all four at once
One deliberately loud example — not a style to actually use, but each change is exaggerated enough that it can only be attributed to one element function.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Vehicles by class") +
  theme(
    # element_text() — anything rendered as text
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold.italic", colour = "firebrick"),

    # element_line() — anything drawn as a line
    panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "darkorange", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed"),

    # element_rect() — anything filled as a rectangle
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightyellow", colour = "black", linewidth = 1.5),

    # element_blank() — removes the element and its space entirely
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )








The title screams “text,” the dashed orange gridlines are obviously a line element, the yellow bordered panel is obviously a rectangle, and the vanished tick marks — not just invisible, genuinely gone, no reserved space — show what element_blank() does that a transparent colour wouldn’t.


5.0.4 One example per functional area
That plot showed how to change things (which element function). This section shows where — one deliberate change per functional area from the section above, each cranked up loud enough to be unmissable, before combining all six at the end.

base_plot <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ year) +
  labs(title = "Vehicles by class and drivetrain, by year")

base_plot








Text. The title, blown up and recoloured well past anything you’d actually ship — impossible to miss, and nothing else on the plot moves.

base_plot +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 28, face = "bold.italic", colour = "deeppink"))








Axis details. Tick marks turned into thick red spikes — the axis text next to them is completely untouched, proving this is a separate area from Text.

base_plot +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "red", linewidth = 4))








Panel. The plotting area itself painted bright yellow — the canvas the bars sit on, not the bars.

base_plot +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "yellow"))








Legend. The swatches blown up to nearly the size of the plot itself.

base_plot +
  theme(legend.key.size = unit(2.5, "cm"))








Facet strips. The panel-label boxes (“1999”/“2008”) lit up bright orange.

base_plot +
  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "orange"))








Plot-level. The entire outer canvas — everything outside the panel — turned hot pink.

base_plot +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "hotpink"))










5.0.5 Putting it together
All six changes on the one chart at once — deliberately garish, but that’s what makes it unambiguous which area each one belongs to.

base_plot +
  theme(
    # Text
    plot.title = element_text(size = 28, face = "bold.italic", colour = "deeppink"),

    # Axis details
    axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "red", linewidth = 4),

    # Panel
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "yellow"),

    # Legend
    legend.key.size = unit(2.5, "cm"),

    # Facet strips
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "orange"),

    # Plot-level
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "hotpink")
  )

title: 6  Colour scales and palettes
text:
6.0.1 Function summary
ggplot’s default hue palette (the muted rainbow you get from just mapping colour/fill with nothing else specified) is fine for a quick look at data, but rarely the right call for anything you’re actually sharing.
This chapter picks a palette deliberately, organised around the shapes a colour variable can take — categorical, ordinal, continuous, and continuous with a meaningful midpoint (diverging) — and for each shows two approaches: colours you supply yourself, and the option currently considered ggplot2’s best-practice built-in for that data shape.
These are formatting functions, applied after the plots structure has been created, changing the colours fed through to the aesthetics that have already been determined. Broadly, functions starting scale_fill affect colours sent to the fill aesthetic, those starting scale_colour affect those sent to the colour aesthetic.x
Every function below is part of ggplot2 itself — none of it requires loading a separate package.
Every function in the table has a scale_colour_*() equivalent alongside its scale_fill_*() version — which one applies depends on the aesthetic the geom uses, not on the function itself.
library(tidyverse)

title: 6  Colour scales and palettes
text:
6.1 Categorical data
Unordered categories (region, product type, drv) — hues just need to be mutually distinct; there’s no “low” or “high.”

6.1.1 scale_colour_manual()
Colours you supply yourself, for the colour aesthetic (points, lines, outlines).

drv_colours <- c("4" = "#1b9e77", "f" = "#d95f02", "r" = "#7570b3")

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = drv_colours)










6.1.2 scale_fill_manual()
Same mechanism, for the fill aesthetic (bars, areas, tiles) — which one you need depends on which aesthetic the geom is using, not on personal preference.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = drv_colours)










6.1.3 scale_colour_brewer()
A named ColorBrewer palette instead of picking colours by hand. Set1/Dark2 are ColorBrewer’s recommendation specifically for points/lines — higher saturation than the palettes meant for filled areas, because a small point or thin line needs more contrast to stay legible than a large filled shape does.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1")










6.1.4 scale_fill_viridis_d()
Built into ggplot2 since 3.0 (2018), and the current default recommendation for categorical data: perceptually uniform and colourblind-safe, sampled at n equally spaced points along the same viridis colourmap used for continuous data below. Unlike a true qualitative palette (Brewer’s Set1/Dark2, or the colourblind-safe Okabe-Ito palette from the separate ggokabeito package), it isn’t capped at a fixed number of categories — but because it’s one continuous ramp rather than colours chosen for mutual contrast, categories get visually closer together as n grows, so it’s best for a handful of groups rather than many.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d()










6.1.5 scale_fill_brewer()
An example of ‘Set1’. Also see ‘Dark2’.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")

title: 6  Colour scales and palettes
text:
6.2 Ordinal data
For an ordered factor specifically — the categories are still discrete, but their order carries meaning (worst to best, low to high), which an unordered qualitative palette can’t communicate.

6.2.1 scale_fill_ordinal()
A direct alias for scale_*_viridis_d(), and what ggplot2 reaches for automatically if you map an ordered factor without specifying a scale. The naming signals intent even though the output is identical to the viridis example above: diamonds$cut is a genuine ordered factor (Fair < Good < Very Good < Premium < Ideal), so the single viridis ramp reads as “worse to better” rather than as arbitrary, mutually-distinct categories the way it would for an unordered factor like drv.

diamonds_cut_counts <- diamonds %>% count(cut)

ggplot(diamonds_cut_counts, aes(x = cut, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_ordinal()

title: 6  Colour scales and palettes
text:
6.3 Continuous data
One variable running low to high (a count, a share, an age), no natural midpoint. Choropleth maps are arguably the clearest real-world case — everyone has seen an election map, and nobody misreads what the “low” and “high” ends of the colour scale mean. USArrests (base R, 1973 US arrest rates by state) plus map_data("state") (state boundary polygons shipped by the maps package — no download, no shapefiles, just data bundled with the package once installed: install.packages("maps")) gives a self-contained version of the same idea.

library(maps)

arrests <- USArrests %>%
  rownames_to_column("state") %>%
  mutate(
    state       = tolower(state),
    murder_diff = Murder - mean(Murder)
  )

arrests_map <- map_data("state") %>%
  left_join(arrests, by = c("region" = "state"))


6.3.1 scale_fill_gradient()
A two-colour continuous ramp, for a plain low-to-high variable with no natural midpoint — the colours themselves are yours to pick.

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = Murder)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "firebrick") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder arrests per 100,000 (1973)", fill = "Rate")










6.3.2 scale_fill_viridis_c()
Built into ggplot2 since 3.0 (2018), and the current default recommendation for continuous data: perceptually uniform (equal steps in the data look like equal steps in colour) and colourblind-safe, properties a hand-picked gradient() isn’t guaranteed to have.

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = Murder)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder arrests per 100,000 (1973)", fill = "Rate")










6.3.3 scale_fill_viridis_b()
The binned equivalent — same continuous Murder variable, but cut into a handful of discrete steps rather than shown as a smooth ramp. Trades precision for legibility: harder to read off an exact value, easier to say “that state is in the third band up.”

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = Murder)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_viridis_b(n.breaks = 5) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder arrests per 100,000 (1973)", fill = "Rate")










6.3.4 scale_fill_fermenter()
Same binning idea, with a Brewer palette instead of viridis — and, like distiller(), needs direction = 1 to read light-to-dark.

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = Murder)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "Blues", direction = 1, n.breaks = 5) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder arrests per 100,000 (1973)", fill = "Rate")

title: 6  Colour scales and palettes
text:
6.4 Diverging continuous data
A variable with a meaningful midpoint (correlation around zero, deviation from an average, agreement scales centred on “neutral”). Same rate as above, re-expressed as each state’s deviation from the national average — “above/below average” is a real, meaningful zero, and it’s an even more natural read on a map than in a bar chart.

6.4.1 scale_fill_gradient2()
A three-colour ramp diverging away from a midpoint, colours supplied directly.

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = murder_diff)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "grey95", high = "firebrick", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder rate vs. national average (1973)", fill = "Deviation")










6.4.2 scale_fill_distiller()
Viridis has no diverging variant, so there isn’t a newer built-in option here than a diverging ColorBrewer palette — scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu") remains the current standard for this case. Unlike gradient2(), distiller() has no midpoint argument: it interpolates the palette evenly across whatever limits the data spans, so centring it means forcing symmetric limits around zero. direction = 1 forces light-to-dark for low-to-high (the conventional reading); distiller() otherwise defaults to -1.

murder_diff_extent <- max(abs(arrests_map$murder_diff), na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = murder_diff)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "RdBu",
    direction = 1,
    limits   = c(-murder_diff_extent, murder_diff_extent)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Murder rate vs. national average (1973)", fill = "Deviation")

title: 6  Colour scales and palettes
text:
6.5 Browsing the full palette range
Both palette families offer more named options than the single examples picked out above — worth browsing directly rather than guessing from a name.

6.5.1 ColorBrewer
The full function family, by data shape:

scale_colour_brewer() / scale_fill_brewer() — discrete
scale_colour_distiller() / scale_fill_distiller() — continuous (interpolates a Brewer palette into a smooth ramp)
scale_colour_fermenter() / scale_fill_fermenter() — continuous data cut into discrete bins first, then coloured with a Brewer palette

Every Brewer palette at once, grouped into its sequential/diverging/qualitative rows.

RColorBrewer::display.brewer.all()










6.5.2 Viridis
The full function family, by data shape:

scale_colour_viridis_d() / scale_fill_viridis_d() — discrete
scale_colour_viridis_c() / scale_fill_viridis_c() — continuous
scale_colour_viridis_b() / scale_fill_viridis_b() — continuous data cut into discrete bins first, then coloured along the viridis ramp

viridisLite (a hard dependency of ggplot2, so already installed — no extra package needed) ships eight colourmaps, selected via the option argument to any scale_*_viridis_*() function: "viridis", "magma", "inferno", "plasma", "cividis", "mako", "rocket", "turbo".

viridis_options <- c("viridis", "magma", "inferno", "plasma", "cividis", "mako", "rocket", "turbo")

viridis_swatches <- map_dfr(viridis_options, function(opt) {
  tibble(
    option   = opt,
    position = 1:20,
    colour   = viridisLite::viridis(20, option = opt)
  )
})

ggplot(viridis_swatches, aes(x = position, y = option, fill = colour)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Viridis colourmap options") +
  theme_minimal()

title: 7  House colour palette
text:
7.1 Hue, tint, and saturation
house_colours (defined in scripts/house_colours.R) is six colour families plus a standalone grey, each a five-step tint ramp — similar in shape to a typical workplace brand-colour template (one base hue per family, tinted from saturated down to pale), but built from independently chosen hues so it stays free of any employer’s brand identity, and safe to use on a public repo.
Every family started out generated — one base hex colour fed through a single function, five tints out the other end. Most of them didn’t stay that way. Getting each family to actually look like a coherent progression of one colour, rather than a smear from vivid to grey or an odd colour clash between neighbouring swatches, meant a lot of hand correction. This chapter is a record of that: the concepts behind the tuning, and the specific pattern each family ended up on.
Three knobs sit behind every colour in this palette, in HSL terms rather than the raw RGB a hex code encodes:
Hue is the position on the colour wheel, 0–360°. It answers “is this blue, or green, or orange” — the colour’s basic identity. Nudging hue is what turned the original straight orange into gold, and it’s the axis a colour family sits on for good: every swatch in a family shares (almost) the same hue.
Saturation is how vivid a colour is versus how much grey is mixed in — 100% is the purest, most intense version of a hue; 0% is plain grey with no colour at all. This is the knob that caused the most trouble in this palette: interpolating a colour straight toward white in RGB space desaturates some hues far faster than others, so a “generated” ramp can quietly go grey in the middle before its swatch count says it should.
Tint is what happens as lightness rises toward white (its opposite, shading, is lightness falling toward black). A five-step tint ramp is a base colour progressively mixed with more and more white. Tint and saturation are easy to conflate — tint necessarily raises lightness, but saturation is a separate axis: two colours can be equally light while one still reads as vivid and the other has gone nearly grey.

title: 7  House colour palette
text:
7.3 Pattern by family
Bases alternate deep and vivid in character: blue and purple sit deep and dark, pink, mint, gold and green sit bright and punchy. Every ramp is capped short of pure white, so even the palest tint still reads as a faint version of its own colour rather than washing out — and the palest swatch of every colour family (not grey) carries a final +8 point saturation nudge over what the ramp would otherwise give, hue and lightness held fixed. At that lightness the maximum possible chroma is small regardless of saturation, so it reads as a gentle lift rather than a dramatic one.
Pink, mint and green share one construction rule. Swatch 1 is the original, untouched base colour — never deepened. Saturation only moves on the swatch5-to-swatch4-to-swatch3 leg, decreasing together with lightness; it then holds flat across swatch3-to-swatch2-to-swatch1, so those three darkest swatches share one saturation and are told apart by lightness alone. That lightness spacing is front-loaded — the widest gap sits between swatch 1 and swatch 2, narrowing toward the pale end — so the flat-saturation trio still reads as clearly distinct steps rather than blurring together.

pink (H330): S90 flat across swatches 1-3, L 50→67→80, then S rising to 100 by the palest swatch
mint (H160): S68 flat across swatches 1-3 (12 points below its neighbours’ pattern - see note below), L 55→70→81, then S pulled back rather than rising - S61→75 across swatches 4-5, both nudges working against the same near-white ceiling from opposite directions
green (H120): S80 flat across swatches 1-3, L 42→62→76, then tapering (rather than holding flat) through the last two swatches — green shares blue/purple’s desaturation problem below, not mint/pink’s easier case

Blue and purple share a different rule, arrived at after several rejected attempts. Both bases have two low, closely-matched RGB channels that rush toward white together under plain interpolation, desaturating fast (blue’s 70% collapses to ~37% by the second swatch if left on the generator; purple’s 65% to ~40%). Dipping saturation right after the base to cushion that collapse — the way purple was originally tuned — fixed the desaturation but then read as washed-out grey through the middle swatches. Holding saturation flat and high all the way through instead read as a distinct, vivid accent colour sitting next to the dark base, not a lighter version of it. The version that stuck: swatch 1 stays a deep, saturated anchor (deeper than any other family’s base), and swatches 2-5 hold hue and saturation essentially flat while lightness alone carries the rest of the ramp — a bold, consistently-saturated group of four lighter tints sitting below one much darker anchor, closer in spirit to how gold works than to a classic dip.

blue (H247): S70 at the base, then a essentially flat S~74-75 across swatches 2-5, L climbing 30→64→77→91→95
purple (H287-292): S67 at the base, then S~62-65 across swatches 2-5, L climbing 40→51→69→87→94

Gold was left on the plain generator — its base saturation already sits near 100%, so there’s no headroom for any of the above corrections to do anything visible. It’s the one family that never needed hand-tuning.
Grey is also generator-only, saturation 0 throughout by definition — differentiated purely by lightness (L 38→51→64→78→91).

title: 7  House colour palette
text:
7.4 Note: the original orange
Gold started out as a straight orange (hue 38°) before its hue was rotated +10° to 48° so it read as gold rather than orange — the same generator, same saturation/lightness/boost recipe, just a different starting hue.

original_orange <- c("#F59B00", "#F7B036", "#F9C56B", "#FBDBA3", "#FFF0D8")
scales::show_col(original_orange, ncol = 5)








Not used anywhere in the current palette, but kept here as a note: this could be reinserted as a seventh family (orange, alongside gold rather than instead of it) or swapped back in for gold if a more literal orange is ever wanted over the current gold.

title: 7  House colour palette
text:
7.5 Note: a “direct” pure-blue alternative
Blue’s base, #231782, sits at hue 247° — genuinely indigo, seven degrees into violet territory rather than the pure blue of hue 240°. Several points in blue’s tuning explored nudging hue back toward 240° or further, rather than accepting that indigo cast. The version actually in use keeps the original indigo hue throughout and never bends it.
As a note only — not used, and not built out with the same care as the real palette — here’s roughly what a “direct” blue would look like anchored on pure blue itself (#0000FF, darkened) instead of the original indigo base, built out with the same flat-hue, flat-saturation, lightness-led shape as the real blue family:

direct_blue <- c("#0000B2", "#3E3EEA", "#8484F0", "#C2C2F4", "#EBEBFA")
scales::show_col(direct_blue, ncol = 5)

title: 7  House colour palette
section: 7.6 The families on the colour wheel
text:
7.6 The families on the colour wheel

hue_ring <- tibble(hue = seq(0, 359, by = 1)) %>%
  mutate(ring_colour = hsv(hue / 360, 0.75, 0.95))

family_hues <- tibble(
  family = c("pink", "mint", "blue", "gold", "purple", "green"),
  hue    = c(330, 160, 247, 48, 291, 120)
) %>%
  mutate(swatch_colour = map_chr(family, ~ house_colours[[.x]][1]))

ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = hue_ring, aes(x = hue, y = 1, fill = ring_colour), width = 1, height = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_point(data = family_hues, aes(x = hue, y = 1.4, colour = swatch_colour), size = 8) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  geom_text(data = family_hues, aes(x = hue, y = 1.75, label = family), size = 3.5) +
  coord_polar(theta = "x", start = 0) +
  ylim(0, 2) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "House palette base hues on the colour wheel")








The two largest empty stretches sit between gold (48°) and pink (330°), or gold and green (120°), as well as between mint (160°) and blue (247°), covering cyan/turquoise/azure.

title: 7  House colour palette
text:
7.7 Each family’s progression
The same five-category variable (diamonds$cut) filled by each family in turn, first as separate bars, then stacked — the stacked version is the harder test, since it’s exactly the situation where neighbouring swatches need to stay distinguishable.

diamonds_clarity_cut <- diamonds %>% count(clarity, cut)


7.7.1 Separate bars

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$pink) +
  labs(title = "pink", fill = "Cut")









ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +

One example per function, reusing the same datasets and chart shapes as the “Colour scales and palettes” chapter, so each house equivalent sits directly next to what it’s standing in for.

7.8.1 scale_fill_house_categorical()

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = as_factor(drv))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_house_categorical(n = 4, primary = 3)








A stacked bar with 6 fill colours, the harder case since neighbouring bands share a border in the same column:

diamonds_clarity_lumped <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(clarity_lumped = fct_lump_n(clarity, n = 5)) %>%
  count(cut, clarity_lumped)

  scale_fill_house_categorical(n = 6, primary = 2) +
  labs(title = "Stacked bar, 6 categorical fill colours", fill = "Clarity")

mpg_manufacturer_lumped6 <- mpg %>%
  mutate(manufacturer_lumped = fct_lump_n(manufacturer, n = 5)) %>%

title: 7  Work-alternative colour palette
text:
7.1 The comparable scale functions
nc_alt1 (from the visu package - see visu/R/nc_alt1.R) is a work-compatible alternative colour palette - five colour families plus a standalone grey, matching the shape of the real work brand palette, so it can be swapped in for it directly. Not the same object as house_colours (this project’s own six-family personal palette) - see visu/R/nc_alt1.R’s own header for the full design rationale.
Same function set as house_colours.R’s (_pal instead of _house), same examples as 6_house_palette.qmd’s equivalents, one each.

title: 7  Work-alternative colour palette
text:
7.1.1 scale_fill_pal_categorical()
For an unordered categorical variable - each level just needs to read as visually distinct from the others, with no implied sequence between them. Draws one colour per family, spreading across hues before repeating within one, same logic as scale_fill_house_categorical(). Grey is a selectable family here (unlike in house_colours), so with enough categories it can turn up as one of the fill colours, not just as a neutral extra.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = as_factor(drv))) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_pal_categorical(n = 4, primary = 4)










7.1.2 scale_colour_pal_categorical()
Same as scale_fill_pal_categorical(), for point/line colour rather than fill - typically a scatterplot with an unordered grouping variable.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = as_factor(drv))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_pal_categorical(n = 4, primary = 1, families = c("blue", "pink", "purple"))










7.1.3 scale_fill_pal_sequential()
For levels that all belong to one colour family rather than being spread across several - e.g. sub-categories of a single concept, where staying within one hue (varying only tint) signals they’re related, rather than distinct topics.
Also the natural fit for an ordered/ranked categorical variable (e.g. a Likert scale, or diamonds$cut’s Fair-to-Ideal ordering) - a single hue’s tint ramp read low to high, so the direction of the order is visible in the colour itself, not just the legend order.
Up to 5 levels, it pulls the family’s 5 discrete shades; past 5 it switches to interpolating continuously between them instead - a family only has 5 real shades to give, so beyond that a discrete tier just isn’t available.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_pal_sequential(family = "orange", n = 3)








diamonds$clarity has 8 ordered levels - past the 5 discrete shades, so this draws on the interpolated branch instead.

diamonds_clarity_counts <- diamonds %>% count(clarity)

ggplot(diamonds_clarity_counts, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_pal_sequential(family = "orange", n = 8)










7.1.4 scale_colour_pal_sequential()
Same as scale_fill_pal_sequential(), for point/line colour.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, colour = drv)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_pal_sequential(family = "blue", n = 3)










7.1.5 scale_fill_pal_gradient()
For continuous numeric data with no meaningful midpoint - a single low-to-high colour ramp, e.g. a raw rate or count mapped onto a map or heatmap.

library(maps)

arrests <- USArrests %>%
  rownames_to_column("state") %>%
  mutate(
    state       = tolower(state),
    murder_diff = Murder - mean(Murder)
  )

arrests_map <- map_data("state") %>%
  left_join(arrests, by = c("region" = "state"))

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = Murder)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_pal_gradient() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder arrests per 100,000 (1973)", fill = "Rate")








family defaults to "pink" (its previous, only behaviour) but takes any nc_alt1 family now.

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = Murder)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_pal_gradient(family = "mint") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder arrests per 100,000 (1973)", fill = "Rate")










7.1.6 scale_fill_pal_diverging()
For continuous numeric data with a meaningful reference point (e.g. zero, or a national average) - two hues diverging in opposite directions from a shared midpoint, so values above and below the reference are immediately distinguishable by colour as well as sign. The one function here that doesn’t take family/families - always pink/mint either side of grey, same as scale_fill_house_diverging().

ggplot(arrests_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = murder_diff)) +
  geom_polygon(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  scale_fill_pal_diverging(midpoint = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Murder rate vs. national average (1973)", fill = "Deviation")

title: 8  House-style building blocks
text:
Once a theme() pass or a ggsave() call gets repeated across charts, it’s worth pulling out into a function rather than copy-pasting the block each time. theme_house() and finalise_plot() now live in the visu package (see BBC’s bbplot for the package version of the same idea this was modelled on: bbc_style() + finalise_plot()).

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(visu)

source("My own colour palette/house_colours.R")


8.0.1 theme_house()
A house theme standing in for a manual theme() pass: consistent title/subtitle/caption sizing, left-aligned title, bottom legend, minor gridlines dropped. No arguments needed beyond an optional base_size.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Vehicles by class and drivetrain", fill = "Drivetrain") +
  theme_house()










8.0.2 Applying it to a finished example
Reusing the diamonds cut-by-clarity chart built up stage by stage in the layering chapter — same data prep, same geoms/scales/coord/facet, theme_house() standing in for the manual 8a–8c theme pass.

diamonds_summary <- diamonds %>%
  count(clarity, cut, color) %>%
  mutate(
    clarity = fct_recode(clarity, "I1 (worst)" = "I1", "IF (best)" = "IF"),
    color   = fct_recode(color,   "D (best)" = "D",   "J (worst)" = "J")
  )

cut_palette <- c(
  "Fair"      = "#b2182b",
  "Good"      = "#ef8a62",
  "Very Good" = "#fddbc7",
  "Premium"   = "#67a9cf",
  "Ideal"     = "#2166ac"
)

plot_house <- ggplot(diamonds_summary, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ color, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Cut composition by clarity, faceted by colour grade",
    x     = "Clarity",
    y     = "Share of diamonds",
    fill  = "Cut"
  ) 

plot_house









plot_house <- plot_house +  theme_house()

plot_house










8.0.3 finalise_plot()
A thin ggsave() wrapper — fixes width/height/dpi in one place so every exported chart is sized consistently, rather than repeating those arguments at every call site.

finalise_plot(plot_house, "figures/diamonds_cut_by_clarity.png")



8.0.4 house_colours
Five colour families plus a standalone grey, each a five-step tint ramp (saturated → pale) generated from one base hue via make_tint_ramp() — same shape as a typical workplace brand-colour template (one base hue per family, tinted down), built from independently chosen hues rather than reproducing one directly.

scales::show_col(unlist(house_colours), ncol = 5)








Bases alternate deep and vivid in character: blue and purple sit deep and dark, pink, mint and gold sit bright and punchy — and every ramp is capped at 85% of the way to white, so even the palest tint still reads as a faint version of its own colour rather than washing out.
Each family applied to the same five-category variable (diamonds$cut), so the six are directly comparable side by side.

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$pink) +
  labs(title = "pink", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$mint) +
  labs(title = "mint", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$blue) +
  labs(title = "blue", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$gold) +
  labs(title = "gold", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$purple) +
  labs(title = "purple", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = cut)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$green) +
  labs(title = "green", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()








A stacked bar check as well — all five cut tints sitting inside the same bar, adjacent to each other, rather than as separate bars. This is a harder test of legibility than the plots above: it’s exactly the situation the palest/darkest swatch pairs need to survive.

diamonds_clarity_cut <- diamonds %>% count(clarity, cut)


ggplot(diamonds_clarity_cut, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$pink) +
  labs(title = "pink", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds_clarity_cut, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$mint) +
  labs(title = "mint", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds_clarity_cut, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col() +

  theme_house()









ggplot(diamonds_clarity_cut, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col() +

ggplot(diamonds_clarity_cut, aes(x = clarity, y = n, fill = cut)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = house_colours$purple) +
  labs(title = "purple", fill = "Cut") +
  theme_house()

  geom_col() +

Same mechanism as scale_fill_manual(), with a named ramp from house_colours swapped in — family picks the family, n trims it to however many levels the variable actually has. See 6_house_palette.qmd’s “The house scale functions” for the fuller set (give_categorical_colours(), give_sequential_colours(), and the scale_*_house_*() wrappers built on them).

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +

mpg_class_drv <- mpg %>% count(class, drv)

ggplot(mpg_class_drv, aes(x = class, y = n, fill = drv)) +
  geom_col() +

title: 9  Basic bar charts
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(visu)


9.0.1 How bar() works
bar() plots statistics already calculated and sitting in a data frame — one row per bar, an x category paired with an already-computed y value (geom_col()’s job) — rather than counting raw observations itself (geom_bar()’s job). dat needs to already be aggregated (e.g. via count() or summarise()) before it’s passed in.

dat — the data frame, one row per bar
x — unquoted column name for the x-axis category
y — unquoted column name for the already-computed value each bar shows
x_lab — optional x-axis title
y_lab — optional y-axis title
title — optional plot title
fill_family — bar colour: an nc_alt1 name ("pink", "blue3"), "multi" (one colour per bar, spread across families), or "<family>_seq" (one shade per bar within a single family — ordered x variables only, max 5 bars)
base_size — base font size in pt, scales all text via theme_house()
horiz — FALSE (default) for upright bars, TRUE to flip horizontal. Whichever of x_lab/y_lab ends up on the narrow left margin gets rotated vertical and wrapped once it’s long enough (3+ characters) — that’s always y_lab when upright, but swaps to x_lab once flipped (see below)
plot_width — feeds the label-wrapping maths only, not the plot’s actual rendered size (see below)
plot_height — feeds the wrapping maths for whichever label is on the left margin (see below)


9.0.1.1 plot_width and plot_height, in more detail
They feed wrap_text()/resolve_y_lab()’s wrapping calculations only — how many characters fit before the x-axis labels, title, or a rotated y-axis title get wrapped — not the plot’s actual rendered size. They only matter once something’s long enough to need wrapping in the first place; short labels and titles won’t react to either. If this were exported via knitting, the chunk’s own fig-width/fig-height options would need to be kept in sync with these by hand — though options exist (e.g. knitr::opts_current$get("fig.width")) to link the two automatically, not yet set up here.



9.0.2 Examples
Same data as 2_geom_gallery.qmd’s geom_col example — one row per class, so bar() can be compared directly against the plain geom_col(fill = "steelblue") version there.

mpg_class <- mpg %>% count(class)



9.0.3 No colour palette
Default fill_family — bar()’s own default, "pink".

bar(mpg_class, class, n)










9.0.4 Bars all the same colour
fill_family given the name of a different nc_alt1 family — still a single colour, applied to every bar.

bar(mpg_class, class, n, fill_family = "blue")










9.0.5 A specific shade
fill_family also takes a family name with a shade number attached (1-5) — resolve_pal_colour() resolves the string, family name alone defaults to shade 1.

bar(mpg_class, class, n, fill_family = "mint4")










9.0.6 Bars different colours
fill_family = "multi" — bar() works out how many bars there are and pulls that many colours from give_categorical_colours_pal() internally, one per bar.

bar(mpg_class, class, n, fill_family = "multi")










9.0.7 Bars coloured sequentially within one family
fill_family = "<family>_seq" — each bar gets a different shade from that one family’s tint ramp instead of spreading across families, for when the x variable is ordered (so the colour progression itself carries meaning). Capped at 5 bars, since a family only has 5 shades — diamonds$cut is a natural fit, an ordered factor with exactly 5 levels.

diamonds_cut <- diamonds %>% count(cut)

bar(diamonds_cut, cut, n, fill_family = "mint_seq", title = "Diamonds by cut")










9.0.8 Custom labels and title
x_lab, y_lab, and title are optional character strings, wrapped to plot_width. A short y_lab (3 characters or under) stays horizontal.

bar(mpg_class, class, n, x_lab = "Vehicle class", y_lab = "Count", title = "Vehicles per class")










9.0.9 Long y-axis label
Past 3 characters, y_lab rotates vertical and wraps to plot_height instead — resolve_y_lab()’s job.

bar(mpg_class, class, n, y_lab = "Number of vehicles in the dataset")








Narrowing plot_height wraps that same label harder.

bar(mpg_class, class, n, y_lab = "Number of vehicles in the dataset", plot_height = 2)










9.0.10 base_size
Scales all text through theme_house().

bar(mpg_class, class, n, title = "Larger base size", base_size = 16)










9.0.11 More categories
bar_width_from_n() widens bars automatically as the category count rises (so they don’t thin out to slivers), and past 8 categories the x-axis labels switch from wrapped/horizontal to a single angled line instead — manufacturer has 15 levels, several with longer names, a harder test than class’s seven short ones.

mpg_manufacturer <- mpg %>% count(manufacturer)

bar(mpg_manufacturer, manufacturer, n, fill_family = "multi", title = "Vehicles by manufacturer")










9.0.12 plot_width
plot_width only feeds the label-wrapping maths (wrap_text()/resolve_y_lab()) — it doesn’t set how wide the plot actually renders. That’s controlled separately, here via the chunk’s own fig-width, or via finalise_plot()’s ggsave() width when exporting rather than knitting. Set both together so the wrapping assumption matches the real output.

bar(mpg_manufacturer, manufacturer, n, fill_family = "multi", title = "A much narrower plot", plot_width = 3)










9.0.13 horiz
horiz = TRUE flips to horizontal bars. Each category gets its own row rather than competing for horizontal space, so the 45° rotation from the previous section doesn’t kick in at all here, even with the same 15-category data.

bar(mpg_manufacturer, manufacturer, n, fill_family = "multi", horiz = TRUE, title = "Vehicles by manufacturer")








Flipping also swaps which label sits on the narrow left margin — a long x_lab now gets the rotate-vertical-and-wrap treatment that y_lab got in the “Long y-axis label” section above, rather than x_lab’s usual plain wrapping.

bar(mpg_manufacturer, manufacturer, n, fill_family = "multi", horiz = TRUE, x_lab = "Manufacturer of vehicle", title = "Vehicles by manufacturer")

title: 10  Clustered bar charts
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(visu)


10.0.1 How bar_clustered() works
Same idea as bar(), but for two categorical variables at once: x groups bars along the axis, fill groups bars side by side within each x group (position = "dodge2"). Colours come from nc_alt1 via scale_fill_pal_categorical(), sized automatically to fill’s number of levels — no fill colour argument to set directly, unlike bar().

dat — the data frame, one row per x/fill combination
x — unquoted column name for the axis grouping
y — unquoted column name for the already-computed value each bar shows
fill — unquoted column name for the within-group colour grouping
x_lab / y_lab / fill_lab — optional axis/legend titles
title — optional plot title
base_size — base font size, via theme_house()
horiz — FALSE (default) for upright bars, TRUE to flip horizontal - done by swapping which column maps to the x/y aesthetic, not coord_flip() (see 9_basic_bar_charts.qmd)
label_digits — decimal places on each bar’s value label, default 1
label_size — font size for value labels, default NULL (falls back to base_size), independent of it
label_style — "normal" (default), "suppress" (no value labels), or "diag" (labels at 45 degrees)
fill_family — NULL (default) colours fill categorically, spread across nc_alt1 families (scale_fill_pal_categorical()); set to a family name (e.g. "mint") to colour it sequentially within that one family instead (scale_fill_pal_sequential()) - suited to an ordered fill variable, no cap on levels
plot_width / plot_height — feed label-wrapping maths only, not the plot’s actual rendered size (see 9_basic_bar_charts.qmd for the fuller explanation)

diamonds cut/color rather than 2_geom_gallery.qmd’s class/drv — that pairing is too sparse to show clustering properly (several classes only have one drivetrain in the data at all, so most “clusters” are really just one bar). Every cut/color combination is well populated, so each cluster actually shows the full comparison.

diamonds_cut_colour <- diamonds %>% count(cut, color)

bar_clustered(diamonds_cut_colour, cut, n, color, title = "Diamonds by cut and colour", fill_lab = "Colour")










10.0.2 The overlap problem, and fixing it
With 7 color levels dodged inside each cut group, the bars get narrow but the value labels stay at base_size regardless, so the numbers collide with their neighbours - visible above. label_size and label_digits are the direct fix: shrinking the label font gives it room to fit, and dropping the decimal (n is a whole-number count, so “.0” is pure wasted width) shortens the text on top of that.

bar_clustered(diamonds_cut_colour, cut, n, color, title = "Diamonds by cut and colour", fill_lab = "Colour", label_size = 6, label_digits = 0)








If that’s still too tight, label_style = "suppress" drops the value labels altogether and leans on the axis/legend instead - a reasonable call once a chart is dense enough that no label size survives gracefully.

bar_clustered(diamonds_cut_colour, cut, n, color, title = "Diamonds by cut and colour", fill_lab = "Colour", label_style = "suppress")










10.0.3 horiz
Flips to horizontal bars - each cut category gets its own row, so the 7 dodged color bars within it have more room top-to-bottom rather than competing for width.

bar_clustered(diamonds_cut_colour, cut, n, color, title = "Diamonds by cut and colour", fill_lab = "Colour", horiz = TRUE, label_size = 6, label_digits = 0)










10.0.4 label_style = “diag”
Rotates the value labels 45 degrees instead - an alternative to shrinking them, for the upright case.

bar_clustered(diamonds_cut_colour, cut, n, color, title = "Diamonds by cut and colour", fill_lab = "Colour", label_style = "diag", label_digits = 0, label_size = 8)










10.0.5 fill_family
color is itself ordered (D best through J worst), so a one-hue sequential ramp (scale_fill_pal_sequential() under the hood) carries that ordering in the colour itself, rather than spreading across families the way the categorical default does. 7 levels is past the 5 discrete shades one family has, so this draws on the interpolated branch.

bar_clustered(diamonds_cut_colour, cut, n, color, title = "Diamonds by cut and colour", fill_lab = "Colour", fill_family = "purple", label_size = 6, label_digits = 0)

title: 11  Stacked bar charts
text:
library(tidyverse)
library(visu)


11.0.1 How bar_stacked() works
Same two-variable shape as bar_clustered(), but stacks segments into one bar per x category (position = "stack") instead of placing them side by side — suited to more x categories, or where the total across fill levels matters as much as each individual segment.

dat — the data frame, one row per x/fill combination
x — unquoted column name for the axis grouping
y — unquoted column name for the already-computed value each bar shows
fill — unquoted column name for the stacked colour grouping
x_lab / y_lab / fill_lab — optional axis/legend titles
title — optional plot title
base_size — base font size, via theme_house()
horiz — TRUE (default, matching this function’s original always-flipped behaviour) for horizontal bars, FALSE for upright - done by swapping which column maps to the x/y aesthetic, not coord_flip() (see 9_basic_bar_charts.qmd)
label_digits — decimal places on each segment’s value label, default 1
label_size — font size for value labels, default NULL (falls back to base_size), independent of it
label_style — "normal" (default), "suppress" (no value labels), or "diag" (labels at 45 degrees)
fill_family — NULL (default) colours fill categorically, spread across nc_alt1 families (scale_fill_pal_categorical()); set to a family name (e.g. "mint") to colour it sequentially within that one family instead (scale_fill_pal_sequential()) - suited to an ordered fill variable, no cap on levels
legend_position — "bottom" (default) or "right"
plot_width / plot_height — feed label-wrapping maths only, not the plot’s actual rendered size (see 9_basic_bar_charts.qmd for the fuller explanation)

Same clarity/cut data as 6_house_palette.qmd’s stacked bar check — flagged there as the harder legibility test, since neighbouring swatches sit right next to each other inside one bar. Also a better fit for bar_stacked() than a smaller grouping: 8 clarity levels justify the horizontal flip.

diamonds_clarity_cut <- diamonds %>% count(clarity, cut)

bar_stacked(diamonds_clarity_cut, clarity, n, cut, title = "Diamonds by clarity and cut", fill_lab = "Cut")










11.0.2 label_digits, label_size, label_style
Same three label arguments as bar()/bar_clustered(). n is a whole-number count, so label_digits = 0 drops the wasted “.0”; stacked segments are usually roomier than dodged bars, but the same label_size/"suppress" options are there if a particular chart gets tight.

bar_stacked(diamonds_clarity_cut, clarity, n, cut, title = "Diamonds by clarity and cut", fill_lab = "Cut", label_style = "suppress")










11.0.3 fill_family
cut is itself ordered (Fair worst through Ideal best), so a one-hue sequential ramp carries that ordering in the colour rather than spreading across families the way the categorical default does.

bar_stacked(diamonds_clarity_cut, clarity, n, cut, title = "Diamonds by clarity and cut", fill_lab = "Cut", fill_family = "mint")










11.0.4 horiz = FALSE
Previously impossible - bar_stacked() always flipped via a hardcoded coord_flip(). Now it’s just the default being overridden, for an upright stacked bar instead.

bar_stacked(diamonds_clarity_cut, clarity, n, cut, title = "Diamonds by clarity and cut", fill_lab = "Cut", 
            horiz = FALSE, label_style = "suppress")








label_style = "diag" on the same upright chart - rotates the segment labels 45 degrees.

bar_stacked(diamonds_clarity_cut, clarity, n, cut, title = "Diamonds by clarity and cut", fill_lab = "Cut", horiz = FALSE, label_digits = 0, label_style = "diag")










diamonds %>% count(cut, color) %>% group_by(cut) %>%
  mutate(p = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  bar_stacked(cut, p, color, y_lab = "Colour (%)", x_lab = "Cut quality", 
              title = "Colour by cut quality")

    data,

    statistics = c("perc"), # Can be "count"
    title = NULL, 
    horiz = F, 
    palette = NULL,
    show_total = T, 
    x_lab = NULL
    ) {
  
  stopifnot(length(statistics) == 1)
  
  if(statistics %in% c("mean", "median")){
    chart_type = "num"} else {chart_type = "cat"}
  
  fill_arg <- "pink"
  
    dat <- 
      calc_stats(
        data       = data,
        outcomes   = outcome,
        predictors = predictor,
        statistics = statistics
        ) 
  
  if(chart_type == "num" & is.null(predictor)){
    
    chart_func <- bar
    x_arg <- sym("o_lab")
    x_lab_arg = x_lab

  } else if (chart_type == "cat" & is.null(predictor)){
    
    chart_func <- bar
    x_arg <- sym("o_cat")
    x_lab_arg <- dat$o_lab[1]
  
  } else if (chart_type == "num" & !is.null(predictor)){
    
    chart_func <- bar
  
  } else if (chart_type == "cat" & !is.null(predictor) & cluster == F){
    
    chart_func <- bar_stacked
    fill_arg <- sym("o_cat")

  } else {chart_func <- bar_clustered}
    
  if(!is.null(predictor)){
    x_arg <- sym("p_cat1")
    x_lab_arg <- dat$p_lab1 %>% grep("Total", ., value = T, invert = T) %>% unique()
    fill_arg <- sym("o_cat")
  }
    
  if(is.null(palette) & identical(chart_func, bar)){palette <- "pink"} 
  
  if(show_total==F & !is.null(predictor)){dat <- dat %>% filter(p_cat1 != "Total")}
  if(statistics == "perc"){dat$estimate <- dat$estimate * 100}

  rlang::inject(
    chart_func(dat = dat, 
                x = !!x_arg, 
                y = estimate,
                fill = !!fill_arg,
                fill_family = palette,
                x_lab = x_lab_arg,
                y_lab = ifelse(statistics %in% "perc", "%", "Count"),

                horiz = horiz
